one_liner: Lean Python 3 implementation for microcontrollers and embedding; about 3.4x faster than Duktape 1.2.2 on 2015 fib(34), slower than PUC Lua.
what_it_does: MicroPython implements Python 3.4 syntax (plus async/await and selected later features) with a subset of the standard library, for microcontrollers and other constrained systems as well as Unix and Windows. It runs .py source or precompiled .mpy bytecode, either from a filesystem or frozen into the firmware. For embedding in a C program, the embed port generates a self-contained set of .c/.h files configured by your own mpconfigport.h. It is a different language from the Duktape baseline (JavaScript), so it competes as the choice of embedded scripting engine, not as a drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: A compact bytecode VM in which every object is one machine word: small ints and interned strings (qstrs) are tagged immediates (MICROPY_OBJ_REPR_A), so integer-heavy code such as fib allocates nothing. MICROPY_OPT_CACHE_MAP_LOOKUP_IN_BYTECODE caches the results of global, name and attribute lookups in the bytecode (enabled in the benchmarked Windows build), and GCC builds can use computed-goto dispatch, which mpconfig.h puts at roughly 10% faster. Per-function @micropython.native and @micropython.viper decorators emit machine code; the docs put native at roughly twice the speed of bytecode, and viper gains more by using machine-word integers.
when_to_use: You want Python syntax for scripting on microcontrollers (esp32, rp2, stm32, samd, mimxrt and others) with as little as 256 KiB flash and 16 KiB RAM.
Embedding a small Python-like interpreter in a C application through the embed port, where CPython is too large.
Recursive or integer-heavy scripting where small-int tagging avoids allocation, with hot functions moved to @micropython.native or @micropython.viper.
Picking a scripting engine against Duktape 1.x-era JavaScript, which used doubles for every number unless built with fastint.
when_not_to_use: Raw interpreter speed: in the same 2015 table PUC Lua (1.341 s) is about 2.1x faster, and AngelScript, Lily, mruby, Squirrel, s7 and NekoVM all finish fib(34) faster.
Code that needs full CPython semantics, the CPython C API or C extensions such as NumPy: only a subset of Python 3 is implemented, and the differences are catalogued in tests/cpydiff.
Long-running, allocation-heavy services on small heaps: open issues report heap fragmentation (#15894, an RP2 web server after 60 h) and super-linear json.dumps on large lists (#19147).
Production Windows hosts: the README of the Windows port calls it experimental and community-supported, and the benchmarked build was that port compiled with MSVC.

integration.form: source-drop (ports/embed generates self-contained .c/.h for a host C project) or standalone firmware or executables per port
integration.dependencies: none for the core; the build uses make, bash and Python 3.3+ (rp2 and esp32 also use CMake), and the microcontroller ports need their vendor SDKs
integration.min_toolchain: gcc per the README (MSVC and mingw-w64 builds exist for the Windows port); Python 3.3+ for the build scripts
integration.platforms: Unix-like (Linux, BSD, macOS, WSL), Windows (experimental port), and over twenty microcontroller ports in three support tiers
integration.thread_safety: Interpreter state is one global (mp_state_ctx), so one interpreter per process; ports with _thread run with or without a GIL depending on MICROPY_PY_THREAD_GIL; @native code does not release the GIL

gotchas: Harness: scriptorium's bench.exe times whole processes launched through system() (cmd.exe and interpreter start-up included; N-1 runs to nul, the last printing to the console), and bench.cc keeps each engine's minimum session average. MicroPython ran in only two sessions, 6.687 s and 2.842 s. In the first session every engine was slower (PUC Lua 2.359 s against 1.341 s later), so compare engines within a session: 2.14x faster than Duktape in session 1 and 3.36x in session 3.

The measured build is MicroPython v1.4.4-90-g9220dc4-dirty (genhdr/mpversion.h, built 2015-07-09) from the experimental Windows port compiled with MSVC, which sets MICROPY_OPT_COMPUTED_GOTO to 0 and turns on MICROPY_DEBUG_PRINTERS and source-line info. Current MicroPython is v1.29.0 (August 2026), and the result says nothing about current builds or microcontroller ports.

The Duktape baseline is handicapped. javascript/duktape/make.bat builds Duktape 1.2.2 with cl /Ox /Oy /MT /DNDEBUG but without DUK_OPT_FASTINT, so every JS number is a double. fib.js also calls a global function, while MicroPython's build caches global lookups in bytecode. The effect of either difference was not measured.

bench.csv also holds four Duktape runs (9.063-9.715 s) in a two-column format that bench.cc's parser drops (it needs three fields). The table's 9.544 s is therefore not Duktape's best run; against 9.063 s the gap would be about 3.2x (derived from page data).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick MicroPython over Lua, mruby, Squirrel or AngelScript when you need Python syntax and ready-made microcontroller ports rather than top interpreter speed, since all of those beat it on this fib test. Among JavaScript-side alternatives, QuickJS or XS beat Duktape by larger and more recent margins.
verified_claims_summary: Third-party 2015 scriptorium shootout on an AMD A10 at 3.8 GHz running Windows 7 64-bit: recursive fib(34), whole process timed through bench.exe and averaged over 5 launches, best session kept. MicroPython 1.4.4 (Windows port, MSVC /Ox) took 2.842 s against 9.544 s for Duktape 1.2.2 (MSVC /Ox, no fastint), about 3.4x faster, and 1.341 s for PUC Lua.
status_note: Very active MIT project (22.1k stars, 9.0k forks, 19,127 commits, last commit 2026-10-02, v1.29.0 released August 2026) that is easy to vendor through the embed port, but the speed evidence is an eleven-year-old single micro-benchmark on an experimental Windows build against a handicapped Duktape baseline.
